questions.prompt: Inside `void f(Widget&& w)`, what is the value category of the expression `w` when passed to `g(w)`?
options: xvalue, because w was declared as Widget&&
prvalue, because rvalue parameters hold temporaries
lvalue, because w is a named variable with an addressable location
glvalue that refuses to bind to either overload
questions.explanation: Value categories belong to expressions, not types. Even though w has declared type Widget&&, the id-expression w names an object with identity, making it an lvalue that calls g(Widget&).

questions.prompt: Which built-in increment expression is well-formed in C++ for `int i = 0;`?
options: int& r = i++;
questions.explanation: Built-in prefix ++i increments i and returns i as an lvalue, so ++ ++i compiles and increments i twice. Built-in postfix i++ produces a prvalue copy, which cannot have its address taken, be assigned to, or bind to int&.

questions.prompt: What are the value category and exact type of the string literal `"lucid"`?
options: prvalue of type const char*
lvalue of type const char[6]
prvalue of type const char[6]
xvalue of type const char(&)[6]
questions.explanation: Unlike integer or floating literals (which are prvalues), string literals have static storage duration and are lvalues of array type const char[N] including the null terminator, which is why &"lucid" compiles.

questions.prompt: Given `int x = 5;`, what types do `decltype(x)` and `decltype((x))` deduce?
options: A is int, B is int
A is int&, B is int&
A is int&&, B is int&
A is int, B is int&
questions.explanation: Under [dcl.type.decltype], decltype applied to an unparenthesized id-expression returns its declared type (int). Parenthesizing it into (x) triggers the general expression rule, yielding int& for an lvalue.

questions.prompt: Given `struct S { int m; int& r; };` and `S make();`, what are the value categories of `make().m` and `make().r`?
questions.code:
struct S { int m; int& r; };
S make();
options: make().m is an xvalue, and make().r is an lvalue
make().m is a prvalue, and make().r is an xvalue
Both make().m and make().r are xvalues
Both make().m and make().r are lvalues
questions.explanation: Under [expr.ref], make() first undergoes temporary materialization ([conv.rval]) to become an xvalue. A non-static data member access on an rvalue yields an xvalue when the member has object type (m), whereas a member of reference type (r) always yields an lvalue.

questions.prompt: In C++17 and later, which statement best describes a class prvalue such as `Widget{42}` before temporary materialization conversion occurs?
options: It is a temporary object allocated in caller stack memory awaiting copy elision
It is an unmaterialized initialization recipe with no object identity or storage address yet
It is an expiring glvalue whose destructor runs at the next comma operator
It is an lvalue stored in static read-only memory
questions.explanation: C++17 redefined prvalues in [basic.lval] as unmaterialized value computations or initializers. A temporary object is only created if temporary materialization conversion ([conv.rval]) is triggered by reference binding, member access, or discarding.
